tip: The linking word o (of) softens the next consonant: plant (children) becomes o blant here.
Roeddwn i fod i means I was supposed to; i fod i marks an arranged or expected action.
Welsh 4 changes by gender: pedwar with masculine nouns like tymor, pedair with feminine ones.
Nouns stay singular after a number: wyth gwestai is literally eight guest, not guests.
hen (old) comes before its noun and softens it: tŷ turns into hen dŷ.
Eleven is un ar ddeg, literally one on ten, from the older base-twenty counting system.
Use mewn for in a or some (indefinite) and yn for in the (definite): mewn tri sir.
Negative past of bod uses doedd with ddim: Doedd hi ddim means she was not.
Roedd is the was or were form of bod for he, she or it: Roedd deg cwestiwn = there were ten questions.
Twenty has its own word, ugain, a leftover of the base-twenty counting system: ugain tŷ.
ei has two meanings: ei (his) softens, ei (her) aspirates. Here ei phlant (her children) shows p to ph.
gweld eisiau means to miss someone, literally to see a want: roedd e'n gweld eisiau = he missed.
wedi plus a verb-noun makes the had-done past: doedd hi ddim wedi clywed = she had not heard.
neb means anyone in a negative sentence and no one otherwise: here ddim plus neb = did not plus anyone.
Soft mutation can delete g entirely: gyrfa (career) becomes ei yrfa (his career).
dy (your, informal) softens the next word: cyfraniad becomes dy gyfraniad.
eu (their) causes no mutation: eu cefnogaeth keeps its c, unlike ei (his) which would soften it.
For that she was, Welsh uses bod: ei bod hi mor hwyr = that she was so late.
Preference is shown with gan: roedd yn well ganddo = he preferred it, literally it was better with him.
yn arfer plus a verb means used to as a habit: roedd hi'n arfer chwarae = she used to play.
Welsh has two you forms: ti (informal) as in gallet ti, and chi (formal or plural).
After rhaid i (someone), the verb softens: brysio becomes frysio in rhaid i ni frysio.
rhaid itself never changes for tense; the bod part does: Rhaid i ni (must), roedd rhaid i ni (had to).
cyn i plus a subject and verb means before someone does: cyn iddi dywyllu = before it gets dark.
dylai means should or ought to: dylai fe ymweld = he should visit.
ar ôl i plus a subject and verb means after someone does: ar ôl iddyn nhw fynd = after they left.
yma (this) and yna (that) sit after the noun: y llyfr yma = this book, yr un yna = that one.
Comparatives use yn fwy (more) plus na for than: yn fwy cyfforddus na'r hen un = more comfortable than the old one.
Unreal conditions pair pe (if) with byddwn i (I would): pe gallwn i ddewis, byddwn i'n byw.
The south says gyda for have: profiad gyda ti = you have experience; the north uses gen or gan.
For longer adjectives, most is mwyaf placed before the word: y person mwyaf cyfeillgar = the friendliest person.
a (and) aspirate-mutates the very next word if it starts p, t or c: papur becomes a phapur.
Ga i (may I or can I have) softens what follows: gweld becomes ga i weld.
